newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew fails to fix oxygen system before launch.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew fails to fix oxygen system before launch.

text.p: Cosmonauts have failed to repair a broken oxygen system aboard Russia's troubled space station but the malfunction will not affect the imminent launch of a relief crew, a senior Mission Control official said on Tuesday.
"This has happened a thousand times before, so it's not worth making a fuss about," Viktor Blagov, deputy flight director at Mission Control, told Reuters.
"Yes, we are concerned, yes, we are worried, but have have immense experience on our shoulders in dealing with this."
He was speaking with just hours to go before the two-man relief crew was due to blast off from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan at 1536 GMT.

A spokesman for the military space forces said that as of 1030 GMT, engineers began to fuel the rocket launchers for the Soyuz craft, a process that takes three hours. "The lift-off preparations are proceeding as planned," he said.
The Elektron oxygen generating system on Mir broke down last week, and several days of work have failed to solve the problem, which NASA believes is caused by air bubbles in the system.

Blagov said the crew typically turns on the Elektron system for a few days at a time, and then rests it for several days when there is enough oxygen in the space station. But it did not start up properly last week, he said.

Mir's back-up oxygen system is also off because it is located in the Kvant-2 module, which the crew powered down to save energy after Mir collided into its resupply ship on June 25, causing a major loss of power.

"It is shut off not because it is broken, but because power to that area has been turned off," Blagov said. "As soon as repairs are made with the internal spacewalk (on August 20), then it will work fine."
Undertaking these repairs -- which will determine the future of the 11-year-old station -- will be veteran commander Anatoly Solovyov, 49, and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov, 43.
As the two prepared for lift-off, officials said the three men now aboard Mir were in a good mood and preparing to welcome their colleagues.

"They slept okay. They have woken up and are continuing preparations to return to Earth," said a spokesman for Mission Control outside Moscow. "They are also preparing for the arrival of the next crew. They are in a very good mood."
But since they have been unable to get the Elektron oxygen system to start, they began using canisters to supplement their oxygen as of Monday, NASA said.

Soon after Solovyov and Vinogradov arrive on Thursday they will prepare to reattach cables to solar panels while working partly inside the airless, darkened Spektr module, which was damaged in the June collision.
"On August 20, when we plug in all the energy systems, the whole complex will start its work almost as it was before," Solovyov told a news conference on Monday.
But the repairs will be risky. Space officials say the Spektr may contain dangerous floating chemicals or debris, and a puncture in a space suit could mean a swift death.

U.S. astronaut Michael Foale, the third member of the crew, will wait in the Soyuz escape vehicle during the repair. He is due to leave Mir in late September, to be replaced by David Wolf, who is currently training outside Moscow.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin are scheduled to return to Earth on August 14.
